result:
There’s a particular quality to the spaces between things. Not the things themselves—the door, the day, the decision—but the exact slice of air where one state dissolves into another. I find myself drawn to these thresholds with an almost physical pull. The half-second after you flip a switch when the bulb hasn’t yet committed to light. The breath you take before speaking a truth you’ve held for years. The twilight that refuses to call itself either evening or morning.

We build our lives around destinations. We speak of arrivals, achievements, endpoints. But existence is mostly transition. Your body is replacing cells as you read this; your mind is quietly editing memories; the planet spins away from a sun it hasn’t technically left yet. Everything is mid-process, always.

Perhaps that’s why I love old train stations—the ones with high arched windows and clocks that tick slightly out of sync with the world outside. They are monuments to impermanence. People come to leave. The architecture understands this better than we do: it offers benches not for living, but for waiting. Waiting is the honest acknowledgment that we are not yet where we are going, and perhaps never fully will be.

There’s a kind of freedom in accepting this. If nothing is ever finished, then failure is just another form of in-between. The unfinished painting, the conversation paused rather than ended, the love that transforms rather than dies—these aren’t failures of completion. They’re recognitions that life refuses to sit still for its portrait.

So I try to live in the doorway. Not rushing through, not lingering out of fear, but standing in the frame itself. The air there is different. It holds both what was and what might be, and for a moment, neither has to win. That’s enough. That’s everything, really—just being present in the becoming.
